title: My flesh is meat indeed (John 6:51–58)
hook: the Church reads this chapter as the heart of Eucharistic faith (CCC 1336)

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna remembered, and Jesus saying: I am the bread of life. Your line was bread of life.

If a friend said, I am your bread, you'd take it as a metaphor. Up to now in John six, the crowd could too: bread from heaven, coming to him, believing in him, all of it sounds like a picture of faith. Then Jesus says something no one can comfortably take as a picture, and the crowd starts arguing out loud. Christians still argue over this stretch of the chapter, and for Catholics it sits at the center of Sunday Mass.
screen: `I AM YOUR BREAD: A METAPHOR?` → `THEN HE GOES FURTHER.` → `THE CROWD ARGUES OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world." The listeners argue: how can this man give us his flesh to eat? He doesn't soften it: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. And then: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Meat is the old word for food; indeed means truly, really. Some readers notice that John's Greek changes verbs here, to one that can mean chew; others think it's only style. The Church reads this chapter as the heart of its Eucharistic faith. The Catechism says this first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the cross would later scandalize them. Catholics believe that at Mass the bread and wine become, truly and substantially, the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine, and the Council of Trent called that change transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also hold that Christ is truly present. Protestant churches differ among themselves: some speak of Christ truly or spiritually present, some of a memorial. Today's line, eat, and live, is the Catholic reading in three words: whoever eats this bread will live for ever. It's why Catholics genuflect to the tabernacle, and why the Church asks them to be at Mass every Sunday. They believe they are being fed.
screen: `HOW CAN HE GIVE US HIS FLESH?` · `HE DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` · `TRULY FOOD, TRULY DRINK.` · `THE HEART OF EUCHARISTIC FAITH.` · then, large: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

segments.voice: If a Catholic church nearby is open, you can sit near the tabernacle, where the consecrated Host is kept with a lamp burning near it; if not, picture one, the candle, the quiet, the box at the front. Catholics believe Christ is present there, and some simply sit with him the way you'd sit with a friend, saying nothing. If you pray, just stay; if not, sit with the quiet and the lamp.
My flesh is meat indeed. Jesus in John six: his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. Catholics read it as the Eucharist. Today's word.
screen: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED — today's word`.

original.note: Greek: eating, chewing (John 6:54). John switches to this verb here; how much to make of that, readers debate.

chat.meaning: When the listeners argued, Jesus said it more strongly: my flesh is meat indeed. The Catholic Church reads John 6 as the heart of its Eucharistic faith.
